idiom_name: plain async use-case function + ORM managed-transaction callback
implementation_notes: Node's core stack has no dependency-injection container, so an application service is an async function (or a small object built at the composition root) that receives its collaborators and delegates the transaction boundary to the ORM's managed-transaction callback: sequelize.transaction(async (t) => ...) and knex.transaction(async (trx) => ...) begin, commit or roll back around the callback, so the service never commits itself. What replaces the classic structure is the closure - the transaction handle lives in the callback scope instead of being a service member - and the service stays stateless and testable by passing fake repositories. A class with explicit begin/commit is justified only when the persistence layer offers no managed-transaction API.
pitfalls: A query that omits { transaction: t } runs on another pooled connection outside the transaction and is not rolled back.
The callback must not swallow errors: returning normally commits whatever happened before.
Long callbacks - awaiting third-party HTTP calls - hold a pooled connection and can exhaust the pool.
